title: Relative Clauses Practice Questions
description: Practice questions on English relative clauses based on the study guide.

questions.question: The woman _____ lives next door is a doctor.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is used for people when functioning as the subject of the clause.

questions.question: The book, _____ is on the table, belongs to the library.
questions.explanation: 'Which' is used for non-defining relative clauses referring to things. 'That' cannot be used after a comma.

questions.question: The student _____ project won the competition is from Haiti.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' indicates possession for people, animals, or things.

questions.question: The man _____ you met yesterday is my uncle.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is used in formal English when referring to a person as the object of the clause.

questions.question: This is the city _____ I was born.
questions.explanation: 'Where' is a relative adverb used to refer to locations.

questions.question: I still remember the day _____ we first met.
questions.explanation: 'When' is a relative adverb used to refer to time.

questions.question: That is the reason _____ she decided to leave early.
questions.explanation: 'Why' is a relative adverb used to refer to reasons.

questions.question: The car _____ I bought last week runs smoothly.
questions.explanation: 'That' is used in defining relative clauses to refer to things.

questions.question: Dr. Jean, _____ research focuses on microfinance, published a paper.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession ('his research').

questions.question: She passed all her exams, _____ surprised her teachers.
questions.explanation: 'Which' can refer back to an entire preceding sentence or clause.

questions.question: The restaurant _____ we had dinner was very crowded.
questions.explanation: 'Where' specifies the location where the action took place.

questions.question: The applicant _____ credentials were verified was hired immediately.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' indicates possession of credentials.

questions.question: The report _____ was published yesterday contains vital data.
questions.explanation: 'Which' (or 'that') refers to things like reports.

questions.question: The year _____ the company was founded was 2010.
questions.explanation: 'When' refers to time ('the year').

questions.question: The entrepreneur _____ you interviewed operates in Gonaïves.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is the object relative pronoun referring to the person being interviewed.

questions.question: Port-au-Prince, _____ is the capital of Haiti, has a vibrant culture.
questions.explanation: In non-defining relative clauses, 'which' must be used for places/things, not 'that'.

questions.question: The dog _____ owner lives upstairs barked all night.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' indicates possession for animals as well.

questions.question: The candidate _____ we recommended got the job offer.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' is used for people in the object position in formal English.

questions.question: The building _____ was damaged in the storm is being repaired.
questions.explanation: 'That' refers to things in defining relative clauses.

questions.question: The moment _____ she announced the winner was unforgettable.
questions.explanation: 'When' is used for time references.

questions.question: My colleague, _____ speaks three languages, led the conference.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is used for people in non-defining relative clauses. 'That' is prohibited.

questions.question: The hotel _____ we stayed offered a beautiful view of the bay.
questions.explanation: 'Where' refers to place.

questions.question: He lost his wallet, _____ forced him to cancel his credit cards.
questions.explanation: 'Which' refers back to the entire clause 'He lost his wallet'.

questions.question: The author _____ latest novel became a bestseller is visiting town.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' indicates possession ('her latest novel').

questions.question: The reason _____ he applied for the grant was clear.
questions.explanation: 'Why' introduces reasons.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The project that we launched last month is successful.'
questions.explanation: The clause specifies which project and is essential to the sentence meaning; no commas are used.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'My colleague, who specializes in AI, gave a presentation.'
questions.explanation: The clause adds extra information, is enclosed in commas, and the main sentence makes full sense without it.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The Eiffel Tower, which is in Paris, is a famous landmark.'
questions.explanation: The information is extra detail enclosed in commas.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'Students who study regularly achieve higher marks.'
questions.explanation: The clause restricts the noun to specific students (only those who study regularly).

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The microfinance institution which operates in Haiti serves 10,000 clients.'
questions.explanation: There are no commas, indicating the clause defines which institution.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The SDGs, which were adopted in 2015, guide global development.'
questions.explanation: The clause adds supplementary information enclosed in commas.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The car that is parked outside belongs to the director.'
questions.explanation: It identifies the specific car; 'that' is used without commas.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'My brother, who lives in Miami, is visiting next week.'
questions.explanation: Commas separate the extra detail about where the brother lives.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The doctor who examined me was very thorough.'
questions.explanation: Essential information identifying which doctor is meant.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'Coffee, which is grown in many tropical regions, is popular worldwide.'
questions.explanation: The clause provides extra non-essential details enclosed in commas.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The house where I grew up has been renovated.'
questions.explanation: It specifies which house is being referred to.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'Her speech, which lasted forty minutes, inspired everyone.'
questions.explanation: The length of the speech is non-essential detail surrounded by commas.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The software that was installed yesterday caused a system error.'
questions.explanation: Essential clause specifying which software caused the issue.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'Professor Williams, whose book won an award, will give a lecture.'
questions.explanation: Extra possessive detail about a named individual set off by commas.

questions.question: Classify the relative clause in: 'The reason why she quit her job remains unknown.'
questions.explanation: Essential clause restricting the noun 'reason'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'My teacher, that is from Canada, speaks French.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. 'That' cannot be used in non-defining relative clauses (with commas). Use 'who' instead.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The book, that I read, was interesting.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. Do not use commas around defining relative clauses, nor use 'that' after a comma.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The woman which called is my aunt.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. 'Which' cannot refer to people. Use 'who' or 'that'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'My friend, lives in Pétionville, is a marketer.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. Relative pronouns cannot be omitted in non-defining relative clauses. It should be 'who lives in Pétionville'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The man who I saw at the market was helpful.'
questions.explanation: Correct. 'Who' (or 'whom'/'that') can be used as object pronouns in informal and everyday spoken English.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The report, which was published yesterday, contains new data.'
questions.explanation: Correct. Non-defining clause correctly uses 'which' and commas.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'This is the laptop, that I bought last week.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. Unnecessary comma before 'that' in a defining relative clause.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The student whose project won is from Haiti.'
questions.explanation: Correct. 'Whose' correctly indicates possession in a defining relative clause.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The manager which hired me left the firm.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. 'Which' is used for things/animals, not people. Use 'who' or 'that'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'She failed the exam, that made her parents upset.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. When referring to a whole preceding clause after a comma, use 'which', not 'that'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The hospital where my sister works is downtown.'
questions.explanation: Correct. 'Where' is correctly used to specify place.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'My uncle, who's house is nearby, is a carpenter.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. 'Who's' means 'who is'. The possessive form is 'whose'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The firm, whose headquarters are in Paris, expanded to America.'
questions.explanation: Correct. 'Whose' can refer to entities/things to show possession.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The place when we met was quiet.'
questions.explanation: Incorrect. 'When' refers to time, whereas 'place' requires 'where'.

questions.question: Is this sentence correct or incorrect? 'The movie that we saw yesterday was thrilling.'
questions.explanation: Correct. Defining relative clause correctly uses 'that'.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The book [that] I read was interesting', can the relative pronoun 'that' be omitted?
questions.explanation: Yes. In defining relative clauses, the pronoun can be omitted if it functions as the object of the clause ('I read [the book]').

questions.question: In the sentence 'The man who called you is my brother', can 'who' be omitted?
questions.explanation: No. 'Who' is the subject of the clause ('who called you'), so it cannot be omitted.

questions.question: In the sentence 'My brother, who lives in Miami, is visiting next week', can 'who' be omitted?
questions.explanation: No. Relative pronouns can NEVER be omitted in non-defining relative clauses.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The song that you played was beautiful', can 'that' be omitted?
questions.explanation: Yes. 'That' is the object of 'played' in a defining clause, so it can be omitted ('The song you played...').

questions.question: In the sentence 'The woman who lives next door is a doctor', can 'who' be omitted?
questions.explanation: No. 'Who' is the subject of 'lives'.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The candidate whom you interviewed was impressive', can 'whom' be omitted?
questions.explanation: Yes. 'Whom' is the object of the verb 'interviewed' in a defining clause.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The Eiffel Tower, which is in Paris, is famous', can 'which' be omitted?
questions.explanation: No. Pronouns cannot be omitted in non-defining relative clauses.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The car that was parked outside was stolen', can 'that' be omitted?
questions.explanation: No. 'That' acts as the subject of 'was parked'.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The food which we ordered arrived late', can 'which' be omitted?
questions.explanation: Yes. 'Which' is the object of 'ordered' in a defining relative clause.

questions.question: In the sentence 'The person whose phone rang left the room', can 'whose' be omitted?
questions.explanation: No. Possessive relative pronouns ('whose') can never be omitted.

questions.question: Combine these sentences using a defining relative clause: 'I met a woman. She works in digital marketing.'
options: I met a woman who works in digital marketing.
I met a woman, that works in digital marketing.
I met a woman, which works in digital marketing.
I met a woman whose works in digital marketing.
questions.correct_answer: I met a woman who works in digital marketing.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces the subject relative clause without commas for a defining relationship.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'The course is online. It focuses on sustainable development.'
options: The course that focuses on sustainable development is online.
The course, who focuses on sustainable development, is online.
The course where focuses on sustainable development is online.
The course whose focuses on sustainable development is online.
questions.correct_answer: The course that focuses on sustainable development is online.
questions.explanation: 'That' or 'which' correctly modifies the non-person noun 'course'.

questions.question: Combine these sentences using a non-defining relative clause: 'Port-au-Prince is the capital. I was born there.'
options: Port-au-Prince, where I was born, is the capital.
Port-au-Prince that I was born there is the capital.
Port-au-Prince, which I was born, is the capital.
Port-au-Prince who I was born in is the capital.
questions.correct_answer: Port-au-Prince, where I was born, is the capital.
questions.explanation: 'Where' introduces the relative clause of location, set off by commas.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'Dr. Jean published a paper. His research focuses on microfinance.'
options: Dr. Jean, whose research focuses on microfinance, published a paper.
Dr. Jean, who research focuses on microfinance, published a paper.
Dr. Jean, whom research focuses on microfinance, published a paper.
Dr. Jean that research focuses on microfinance published a paper.
questions.correct_answer: Dr. Jean, whose research focuses on microfinance, published a paper.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' replaces the possessive pronoun 'his'.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'The project was successful. We launched it last month.'
options: The project that we launched last month was successful.
The project, that we launched last month, was successful.
The project who we launched last month was successful.
The project where we launched last month was successful.
questions.correct_answer: The project that we launched last month was successful.
questions.explanation: 'That' correctly connects the object relative clause without commas.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'The girl won the prize. Her mother is an architect.'
options: The girl whose mother is an architect won the prize.
The girl who mother is an architect won the prize.
The girl, that mother is an architect, won the prize.
The girl whom mother is an architect won the prize.
questions.correct_answer: The girl whose mother is an architect won the prize.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' replaces 'her' to show possession.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'I visited the village. My grandparents live there.'
options: I visited the village where my grandparents live.
I visited the village when my grandparents live.
I visited the village who my grandparents live.
I visited the village whose my grandparents live.
questions.correct_answer: I visited the village where my grandparents live.
questions.explanation: 'Where' replaces 'there' to indicate place.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'She passed her exam. This surprised everyone.'
options: She passed her exam, which surprised everyone.
She passed her exam, that surprised everyone.
She passed her exam where surprised everyone.
She passed her exam, who surprised everyone.
questions.correct_answer: She passed her exam, which surprised everyone.
questions.explanation: 'Which' after a comma refers back to the whole situation ('She passed her exam').

questions.question: Combine these sentences: 'The company hired a consultant. You recommended him.'
options: The company hired the consultant whom you recommended.
The company hired the consultant which you recommended.
The company hired the consultant, that you recommended.
The company hired the consultant whose you recommended.
questions.correct_answer: The company hired the consultant whom you recommended.
questions.explanation: 'Whom' (or 'who'/'that') refers to the consultant as the object of 'recommended'.

questions.question: Combine these sentences: '2015 was the year. The Sustainable Development Goals were adopted then.'
options: 2015 was the year when the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.
2015 was the year where the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.
2015 was the year which the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted then.
2015 was the year whose the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.
questions.correct_answer: 2015 was the year when the Sustainable Development Goals were adopted.
questions.explanation: 'When' replaces 'then' to refer to a time period.
